hero.title: A place for your teen's own perspective.
hero.summary: Explore support around school, relationships, identity, and emotional strain, with room for the teen's voice and a clear conversation about privacy and participation.

panel.title: Understand the care before choosing a time.
paragraphs: Read about the work, compare clinicians, and choose the starting appointment that fits. A request is not a confirmed booking.

items.title: How the first conversations work
items.text: Start with the process, not a list of labels.

items.title: Your questions, answered
items.text: Format, participation, and practical next steps.

sections.title: Support should make room for the person growing through it.
paragraphs: A teen may be dealing with several questions at once: how to meet expectations, where they belong, what they want to share, and which parts of life feel under their control. The person seeking the appointment may be a caregiver, but the teen's own description needs room too.

This guide offers ways to understand a starting conversation, not a checklist that decides whether a teen needs therapy. NIMH advises attention when emotional or behavioral concerns persist, cause distress, or interfere with everyday functioning. An evaluation can clarify what is happening and what kind of help fits.

Teen counseling should not be presented as a place to make someone agree with a parent, reveal everything, or perform a version of wellness. The first useful step may be understanding the disagreement about what help would actually mean.

panel.title: For the teen: you can bring questions, too.
paragraphs: You can ask what the appointment is for, what happens if you do not know what to say, and how the clinician handles disagreement.
You should receive an explanation of privacy and its limits. This page cannot promise that everything stays confidential in every situation.

sections.title: Make a broad concern more specific.

items.title: Pressure and overthinking
items.teaser: When school, expectations, or future decisions take up too much space.
paragraphs: A starting question could be whether the difficulty is beginning a task, coping with a possible mistake, or carrying work into the rest of the day. Those examples point to different conversations. You do not need to decide on a clinical label before asking about support.
Describe what a more manageable week would look like from the teen's perspective, not only from a grade or attendance record.

items.title: Belonging and identity
items.teaser: When fitting in and being yourself feel hard to hold together.
paragraphs: A teen might want to talk about friendships, expectations, identity, or a boundary. An open question leaves room for an answer you did not predict. It is different from asking a therapist to confirm what an adult already believes is wrong.
Caregiver concerns can be important without becoming the only account of the teen's experience.

items.title: Communication at home
items.teaser: When even a practical question becomes a conflict.
paragraphs: In a fictional example, a request for an update about plans is heard as mistrust, while silence is heard as disregard. The useful question is what each person is asking for and how that conversation unfolds, not which label belongs to the teen.
Individual teen care and family sessions are different options. A clinician can help clarify which service fits rather than combining them without discussion.

sections.title: Two viewpoints deserve a clear agreement.

items.title: For teens
paragraphs: Ask what choices you have within sessions, how goals are set, and how to say that a question or activity does not fit. Being uncertain is information, not a failure to participate.
Before sharing sensitive details, ask what may be communicated to caregivers and in what circumstances. The actual consent discussion matters more than assumptions based on this page.

items.title: For caregivers
paragraphs: Bring your observations and concern, but leave room for a different description. Ask what role is proposed for you and how practical updates, safety concerns, and between-session communication will work.

Do not assume therapy produces a report of everything said. Equally, do not rely on a website to establish specific legal confidentiality rights; the clinician should explain the applicable arrangements.

sections.title: A beginning that does not require all the answers.

items.title: Check the fit
paragraphs: Confirm that the clinician works with the teen's age and the requested service. Discuss in-person or online participation, the first appointment, and practical access needs.

items.title: Agree on the purpose
paragraphs: The starting conversation can distinguish the adult's concern from the teen's goals. A useful working question may become clearer after listening rather than being fixed before the first visit.

items.title: Review the experience
paragraphs: Ask how the plan can be revisited when a session feels unhelpful or a task does not fit everyday life. Progress should involve the teen's perspective, not just compliance with an outside expectation.

sections.title: The same school day can mean different things to different people.

items.title: What a caregiver notices
paragraphs: In this fictional example, a caregiver sees missing homework and wants a plan for getting it done.

items.title: What the teen describes
paragraphs: The teen describes feeling overwhelmed by the morning, worrying about a friendship, and not knowing how to ask for help. Neither description alone explains the whole situation.

items.title: What the conversation opens
paragraphs: A first discussion could clarify what each person has noticed and what further assessment is useful. It need not begin by choosing one account and dismissing the other.

reveal.title: What makes this a starting point, not an answer?
paragraphs: A clinician would need to understand the specific situation, not infer a diagnosis or explanation from homework alone. The next step might involve the teen, caregivers, school context, or a different referral, with roles and privacy discussed explicitly.
This fictional example illustrates why the teen needs a voice in the conversation; it does not prescribe a family exercise or tell you what is happening for your teen.

sections.title: Find a clinician whose work fits your next step.
sections.intro: These profiles describe working with teens. Read the biography and confirm the current service, age range, and availability.

sections.title: Answers before you begin.

items.question: What if my teen does not want to talk?
paragraphs: Ask the clinician how they handle reluctance and what the initial service would involve. You can describe the uncertainty before arranging a visit. Avoid promising that silence will be punished or that a therapist will make the teen reveal something.

items.question: Is teen counseling the same as family therapy?
paragraphs: Not necessarily. Teen counseling may focus on the young person's goals while involving caregivers as appropriate. Family therapy brings the relationships and participating family members into the work more directly. Ask who the client is and what service is being proposed.

items.question: Can a teen choose their clinician?
paragraphs: You can review profiles together or let the teen identify questions about style and fit. Actual availability, age range, consent, and service requirements still need confirmation. A good-looking profile alone does not establish that the appointment is appropriate.

items.question: How do online appointments work for a teen?
paragraphs: Ask about a private place, a reliable connection, and who should be nearby or available. Joining while driving or in a space where someone cannot speak freely is not a workable plan. The clinician needs to confirm the format and physical-location eligibility.

items.question: What if the main concern is school?
paragraphs: Describe the concern without assuming that therapy replaces school support or educational evaluation. Ask whether coordination would be useful, who would be involved, and what consent is needed. No records are shared because someone reads this page.

items.question: Where should we turn if safety cannot wait?
paragraphs: An ordinary scheduling request is not an urgent response. For a mental health crisis, call or text 988 in the U.S. If someone is in immediate danger or has a life-threatening emergency, call 911.

sections.contact: For practical questions, [email support@mft.care](mailto:support@mft.care?subject=Service%20question). Please leave private clinical details out of the initial email.
